new_statements.rule_in_words: Sandawe is described purely as a lexical tone language (underlying H vs L on morae/syllables, with downstep, tone spread and largely predictable tone melodies); none of the five accessible primary descriptions posits word stress or an accent position. The only stress remark is that Swahili penultimate stress is borrowed as a Sandawe high tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Kagaya 1993 (intro) notes the vowel of a word-initial syllable tends to be lengthened in isolation forms; Elderkin 1989 and Steeman 2012 describe word-level pitch registers ('word levels') assigned by syntax/information structure, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statements concern the phonological word (root/stem plus suffixes and clitics); downdrift applies within the phonological word (Steeman 2012 p. 48). No citation-form stress domain is defined because no stress is described.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Sandawe (sand1273, ISO sad). Hunziker, Hunziker & Eaton 2008 is based mainly on one speaker from Magambua (western dialect); Eaton 2010 and Steeman 2012 draw on both western and eastern dialect speakers. No separate dialect glottocodes involved.

sources.note: No section or statement on word stress/accent in Sandawe; ch. 4 (pp. 28-60) analyses lexical tone (underlying H and L, mora as TBU, downstep, tone melodies, tone spread). Only stress mention (p. 51): Swahili loans map the Swahili stressed penult onto a Sandawe high tone, flanked by lows.

sources.citation: Eaton, Helen. 2010. A Sandawe grammar. SIL e-Books 20. Dallas: SIL International. 206 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 1.3 Phonological overview (pp. 9-11): 'Sandawe has two underlying tone levels: high and low' with downstep, tone spread, tone melodies; the word 'stress' never occurs; 'prominence' (12.4) is discourse-level morphological marking, not phonological stress.

sources.citation: Steeman, Sander. 2012. A grammar of Sandawe: a Khoisan language of Tanzania. PhD Leiden / LOT Dissertation Series 295. 280 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 2.4 Tone (pp. 37-52): two level tones H and L plus rising contour, syllable as TBU, downdrift/downstep within the phonological word; no stress or accent section, all occurrences of 'stress' are the ordinary verb.

sources.citation: Elderkin, Edward Derek. 1989. The significance and origin of the use of pitch in Sandawe. DPhil thesis, University of York. 332 pp.
sources.note: Whole thesis on pitch: lexical two-height tone system with the mora as tone-bearing unit (ch. II.H, pp. 79-88), plus syntactically assigned word pitch levels (ch. III). No statement about word stress; 'stress'/'accent' do not occur as prosodic terms in the scanned text.

sources.citation: Elderkin, Edward D. 1991. Clause structure and tone in Sandawe. York Papers in Linguistics 15: 93-115 (ERIC ED338065).
sources.note: Tone levels of words within the clause; nothing on word stress.

sources.note: Intro sec. 2 'Tones': 'this language is one of the tone languages, and there are four tones' (H, L, rising, falling, plus possible mid/downstepped H). No stress statement; notes only that the vowel of a word-initial syllable tends to be pronounced long in isolation.
